svg.title: VPNv4 route reflector design: the six rules that decide whether the control plane survives
svg.desc: Left: a cluster with two route reflectors and three clients, showing that clients peer only with the reflectors and that the two reflectors must share a cluster ID so loop prevention is consistent. Right: six rules with the reason for each. Rule one, never let a router reflector also act as a PE on a large network, because client load competes with forwarding. Rule two, two reflectors per cluster, in different failure domains. Rule three, one cluster ID per cluster. Rule four, clients must not peer with each other, or the loop-prevention attributes stop being authoritative. Rule five, place reflectors in the core where the IGP cost to all clients is symmetric. Rule six, the reflector changes no attributes, so an outbound policy that strips route targets will break every client at once. A closing note explains that a reflector is a control-plane device and should be sized on routes and sessions, not on bandwidth.
svg.text: A reflector is a control-plane device; size it in routes and sessions, not in bandwidth
Six rules, each of which exists because of a failure someone already had
ONE CLUSTER, TWO REFLECTORS
RR-1
RR-2
same cluster ID 1.1.1.1
different failure domain
PE-A
PE-B
clients
PE-C
Clients peer with both reflectors, never with each other.
THE SIX RULES
1. Do not combine RR and PE on a large network. Client load competes with forwarding.
2. Two reflectors per cluster, in separate failure domains, both configured.
3. One cluster ID per cluster. A mismatch defeats cluster-list loop detection.
4. Clients must not peer with each other; otherwise the attributes are not authoritative.
5. Put reflectors in the core, where IGP cost to every client is symmetric.
6. A reflector rewrites nothing. Outbound policy that strips RTs breaks all clients at once.
Loop prevention, as the reflector sees it
Originator ID: the original advertising router.
Cluster list: every cluster the route has passed.
If either says “been here”, the route is dropped.
Sizing check: the reflector holds every VPNv4 route for every client, so memory and update generation are the limits, not interface speed.
Before adding a 40th VRF, compute the route count the reflector will hold. “It works today” is not a capacity plan for next quarter.
